transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-02
Start: 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~78 minutes
Attendees: Sara Kim (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Marco Ruiz (Orion CTO), Dr Anita Shah (Platform Eng), Ellen Park (SRE), Vikram Patel (ML Eng)

Summary:
Quick technical deep dive focused on stability incidents: CUDA OOMs on private deployment, intermittent timeouts on hosted API, retry semantics and idempotency, KV cache evictions causing performance cliffs, and recommendations around quantization and batching to reduce memory pressure. Customer shared recent incident timeline and logs; Redwood SEs proposed instrumentation, guardrails, and short-term mitigations (smaller batch sizes, eviction thresholds, pinned memory tuning) and medium-term fixes (kernel selection flags, allocator tuning, retry/backoff policy changes).

Topics:
- OOM patterns and memory fragmentation
- CUDA errors & driver/kernel mismatches
- Request timeouts and retry semantics (idempotency concerns)
- KV cache behavior and eviction cascades
- Batching strategy and per-request backpressure
- Quantization tradeoffs and inference stability
- VPC/on-prem constraints for debugging/telemetry

Action items (captured in metadata above).

Transcript:
[00:00] Sara Kim: hey everyone thanks for carving out the time, we'll try to keep this focused, um, the goal is to walk through the incidents you saw last week and dig into root causes and mitigations.
[00:12] Marco Ruiz: thanks sara, yeah it's been rough for us, we had three spikes of OOMs across 2 clusters and some production jobs just got killed mid-request which is, yeah, pretty bad.
[00:23] Ellen Park: and sometimes the request just timed out client-side, retries made things worse and then we saw a cascade.
[00:31] Liam O'Connor: ok, thanks, can you give us a short timeline of when the first OOMs started and what workloads were running?
[00:41] Marco Ruiz: sure, first hit around 02:15 UTC last tuesday, running our nightly report generator (long context, about 8k tokens average) using the private deployment in our VPC. We had batching turned on, batch size 8, dynamic padding. At the same time we had a couple of QA jobs hitting the same nodes.
[01:02] Vikram Patel: just to interject, we were also trying out 4-bit quantized model variant to save costs — the model was a custom fp16->4bit pipeline using the quantizer from the community repo.
[01:11] Priya Nair: ok interesting, mixing experimental quantization with production batching is a classic risk factor. Did you see cuda out of memory messages in dmesg or the container logs?
[01:22] Dr. Anita Shah: yes, our logs show repeated "CUDA out of memory" and also a couple of messages that looked like cublas attempts failing then a full allocator error. Some logs say "CUDA error: out of memory" and others show "cuBLAS: CUBLAS_STATUS_ALLOC_FAILED".
[01:39] Liam O'Connor: that aligns — two likely sources: (1) transient peaks because of large KV cache growth for long context sequences, (2) fragmentation due to mixed allocation patterns with quantized kernels using extra scratch buffers.
[01:54] Marco Ruiz: when you say KV cache growth, are you referring to the prefix caching that stores past attention states? We do have some long-running chat sessions that keep accumulating.
[02:05] Liam O'Connor: yep that's the one — KV cache retention + per-request cache replicas per worker can push memory up. Also if your batching policy is continuous batching with variable sequence lengths, the effective peak memory of a batch can be much larger than average.
[02:19] Ellen Park: in our case we saw 3–4 concurrent long-context sessions plus the batch of 8; maybe we didn't account for the extra per-session overhead.
[02:28] Sara Kim: quick q — do you run shared workers (multi-tenant on node) or one session per GPU?
[02:34] Marco Ruiz: multi-tenant, we have 2 apps colocated right now.
[02:37] Priya Nair: multi-tenant plus quantized experimental kernels — and likely different allocators — can create fragmentation. Also mismatch between the model's expected torch quantized kernels and runtime kernel selection can allocate temporary CUDA tensors in full fp32 scratch for some ops.
[02:56] Vikram Patel: hmm we did see intermittent cudaMalloc failures in startup logs earlier but we blamed it on ephemeral startup noise.
[03:04] Liam O'Connor: startup failures are a hint — the runtime tries to warm kernels and allocate workspace; if those fail once, you can leave the GPU in a state where subsequent allocations are more likely to fail (driver-level fragmentation).
[03:17] Marco Ruiz: what about timeouts? we saw the client side time out, retry, and then those retries increased load and triggered more OOMs.
[03:26] Priya Nair: classic feedback loop — retries without backoff + no idempotency tokens cause duplicate in-flight requests which double memory pressure. Does your client implement idempotency keys or backoff?
[03:37] Ellen Park: no idempotency keys currently; our SDK-level retry is simple immediate retry 3x.
[03:43] Liam O'Connor: that's risky in constrained memory situations. Best practice: short client timeout + exponential backoff and idempotency tokens for mutating operations (but for inference it's still helpful to avoid duplicates). Also server-side we support retry deduplication on the request ID if you pass a client-generated uuid.
[04:02] Marco Ruiz: okay, we'd have to change a lot of clients, but that's feasible. In the short term, is there a server-side mitigation?
[04:09] Sara Kim: yes, you can enable request-level admission control to reject new large-context requests when memory is close to threshold; also can set per-model concurrent request limits.
[04:18] Priya Nair: and on Redwood Dedicated / Private we can modify eviction thresholds for KV cache: shrink prefixes older than X seconds or limit per-session KV allocation. That reduces steady-state memory.
[04:32] Vikram Patel: is there a way to write KV cache to host pinned memory and swap in only needed keys?
[04:40] Liam O'Connor: we do a hybrid — metadata/pointers on host pinned memory and hot KV on GPU. But the copy overhead can add latency if not tuned. For large contexts this is a tradeoff between latency and memory safety.
[04:54] Ellen Park: our latency SLO is 300ms for interactive; swapping would blow that.
[04:59] Priya Nair: right, swapping is more of a batch/offline fallback. For interactive you want tight cache budget and smaller batch sizes.
[05:07] Marco Ruiz: you mentioned kernel selection flags. can you expand?
[05:11] Liam O'Connor: sure — our runtime picks kernels based on architecture and sequence length. For quantized paths there are multiple kernels: one optimized for short sequences that uses less temporary workspace and another that fuses operations but needs a larger scratch buffer. If the runtime picks the larger kernel for a mix of sequences it'll allocate the bigger scratch once and that can push you over OOM. We can force kernel policy to favor lower-scratch kernels for your workload.
[05:38] Marco Ruiz: that sounds promising. How invasive is that change?
[05:41] Liam O'Connor: non-invasive — it's a config flag per model or per deployment. We can run a bench to profile which kernel choice yields better tail latency vs memory.
[05:51] Ellen Park: about the CUDA errors — we saw sometimes a driver stack trace referencing a different CUDA driver version than the container image expected. could that cause instability?
[06:00] Priya Nair: yes, driver/runtime mismatches can cause non-deterministic allocation failures. Are you on a mix of host drivers across nodes?
[06:07] Marco Ruiz: hm, possibly — we had a node reimage last month and might not have homogenized drivers.
[06:12] Liam O'Connor: that would be high on the checklist — ensure driver/kernel and cuDNN/cuBLAS versions are consistent. We also recommend enabling the runtime's driver compatibility checker in private deployments; it logs mismatches and decommissions nodes for probing.
[06:27] Vikram Patel: can the runtime automatically fallback to CPU for a request if GPU allocations fail?
[06:33] Liam O'Connor: currently we have a graceful fallback policy for compatible model variants (smaller quantized model or CPU path) but auto-fallback mid-request is risky for latency and complexity. We usually do pre-checks and route to an alternate model instance if memory pressure is high.
[06:48] Marco Ruiz: what about retries and client-facing timeout semantics — we want to avoid duplicate work but still have good user experience.
[06:56] Sara Kim: recommended pattern: client timeout < server soft-timeout, server responds with IN_PROGRESS token quickly for longer running jobs, or you adopt streaming so the client sees progress. Additionally, server-side helps by deduping via request id and queueing with admission control.
[07:14] Dr. Anita Shah: we use WebSockets for some interactive flows, migration to streaming might be non-trivial for our web app.
[07:22] Priya Nair: streaming isn't required; even short keepalives or progress updates reduce retries. But ultimately, make the retry policy exponential with jitter and include idempotency key.
[07:33] Marco Ruiz: ok. For the concrete OOM case, what are the top three immediate mitigations we can apply with minimal code change?
[07:41] Liam O'Connor: 1) reduce batch size from 8 to 4 for long-context routes; 2) enable KV cache eviction policy (LRU with per-session cap); 3) enforce client idempotency + exponential backoff.
[07:53] Ellen Park: that seems doable. Any config we can flip now?
[07:57] Sara Kim: yes we'll provide the exact flags; Liam will include recommended values.
[08:01] [00:08:01] Marcus (note: mislabelled) Speaker 1: um sorry, quick question, have you considered quantization-aware training vs post-training quant?
[08:10] Vikram Patel: we used post-training 4-bit, not QAT.
[08:13] Liam O'Connor: QAT tends to be more stable and reduces need for fallback kernels, but it's heavier. If you can't re-train, run the quantized variant in a smaller fleet or with stricter eviction.
[08:26] [00:08:26] Ellen Park: several of our errors reference 'nvml' reporting memory spikes — can that be false positive?
[08:33] Priya Nair: nvml is usually reliable but look at per-process resident set size and also sample with device-side allocator traces; sometimes pinned host allocations show up differently.
[08:43] Marco Ruiz: how about GC on the python side? could garbage collection pauses cause allocations to pile up?
[08:49] Liam O'Connor: yes, if many large CPU-side tensors aren't freed promptly you can see sudden surges once they get copied to GPU. We recommend explicit del + torch.cuda.empty_cache in warmup or use the runtime's memory pool which reduces spikes.
[09:03] Vikram Patel: do you recommend jemalloc or tcmalloc in our environment?
[09:07] Priya Nair: tcmalloc tends to be better at reducing fragmentation for our workloads, but we should bench.
[09:12] Marco Ruiz: can Redwood help run a bench with our trace data?
[09:16] Sara Kim: yes that's what the bench next week is for — SE-led, we'll replay traces against kernel policies and quantization variants.
[09:25] [00:09:25] Ellen Park: on the topic of retry semantics, do you persist requests to disk to de-duplicate across restarts?
[09:32] Liam O'Connor: not by default in the hosted API, but in Private we can enable durable request journal for critical endpoints that survive restarts and dedupe. It does add disk overhead and I/O latency so it's opt-in.
[09:46] Marco Ruiz: we might opt-in for the nightly report generator but not for real-time interactive.
[09:53] Priya Nair: sensible. For nightly off-peak jobs a durable journal plus CPU fallback could avoid OOMs altogether.
[10:01] [00:10:01] Vikram Patel: curious about the 'automatic batching' behavior — is it possible it batched unrelated long-context sessions together increasing peak memory?
[10:09] Liam O'Connor: yes if you use a single batcher with no grouping by sequence length, unrelated sessions can be packed together. We support grouping keys (e.g., context-length buckets) to avoid mixing very long contexts with short ones.
[10:23] Marco Ruiz: do you recommend static bucket sizes?
[10:26] Priya Nair: dynamic bucketing is better — maintain a small set of bins (short/medium/long) and limit max batch size per bin. That keeps tail memory bounded.
[10:36] Ellen Park: we've also seen intermittent 'NCCL timeout' when multiple GPUs sync — could that tie into OOM?
[10:42] Liam O'Connor: it can. If one GPU runs out of memory mid-allreduce, other ranks can block and then time out. In multi-GPU or multi-node setups ensure homogeneous memory budgets and guard against OOM injection.
[10:55] Marco Ruiz: are there debugging hooks we can enable?
[10:58] Sara Kim: yes we'll send a debug config: leveled logging (allocator, kernel selection), nvprof traces, and a small agent to gather nvml/per-process metrics periodically. Also a flag to produce heap dumps on cudaMalloc failures.
[11:13] Vikram Patel: that heap dump would be very helpful.
[11:16] [00:11:16] Ellen Park: regarding quantization — we saw output quality regressions sometimes when falling back to another kernel; is that expected?
[11:24] Priya Nair: it can happen if kernels implement numerically different reductions or if we mix quantized vs fp16 kernels in a fused op. We'll test for regressions and pin model variants during rollout.
[11:35] Marco Ruiz: for our compliance team we also need to capture audit logs and stack traces — will these debugging hooks capture sensitive data?
[11:43] Sara Kim: debug traces are configurable at collection time and we redact prompt content by default; raw traces can be kept on your private S3 if needed for incident review.
[11:55] Dr. Anita Shah: good. For on-prem debugging, can Redwood access nodes or do we need to provide bundles?
[12:02] Liam O'Connor: for Private we do an agent-based collection; we don't require remote SSH into your cluster — you can run the agent and upload bundles to a secure session link. We also offer a supervised debug session if you prefer live troubleshooting under NDA.
[12:18] Marco Ruiz: we'll probably choose an upload bundle first.
[12:21] [00:12:21] Priya Nair: ok, let's pivot to concrete reproduction steps for the bench: please provide a representative trace of incoming requests (timestamps, lengths, batching hints), a small sample of logs around the OOM window, and the node spec (driver versions, GPU model, kernel). We'll replay with three kernel policies and two quantization variants.
[12:41] Vikram Patel: we can share that. Ellen will pull logs.
[12:45] Ellen Park: noted, I'll extract logs and forward them.
[12:48] Sara Kim: quick question on SLOs — can you tolerate increased p99 latency during the pilot?
[12:53] Marco Ruiz: for the nightly reports yes; for interactive we need to keep p95 under 300ms.
[12:59] Liam O'Connor: then bench will focus on p95 targets for interactive paths and p99 for batch routes.
[13:06] [00:13:06] Marco Ruiz: any further tips about retries? we've been thinking about client-side token bucket throttles.
[13:12] Priya Nair: token bucket is good. Combine with server-side admission control and per-route concurrency limits. Also, long-context routes should have tighter client quotas.
[13:24] Ellen Park: what about CUDA memory pool settings in torch? should we set TORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF?
[13:30] Liam O'Connor: yes set TORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=max_split_size_mb:128 to reduce fragmentation for small allocations; but values depend on workload. We'll suggest a conservative value in the config we send.
[13:42] Vikram Patel: are there any known issues with the community 4-bit quantizer we used?
[13:46] Priya Nair: some community quantizers rely on custom kernels that may not be fully optimized for recent driver stacks; they may fallback to slower paths or allocate large scratch buffers. That's a risk.
[13:58] Marco Ruiz: ok. For the bench next week, can we also test a non-quantized fp16 baseline so we can see regression in tail latency?
[14:05] Sara Kim: absolutely. We'll do fp16, community 4-bit, and our recommended 4-bit profile.
[14:12] [00:14:12] Dr. Anita Shah: any final comments on metrics to collect?
[14:16] Liam O'Connor: we want per-request GPU memory usage, nvml samples, allocator traces, kernel selection logs, queue length, batch size distributions, and request ids for dedupe analysis.
[14:29] Ellen Park: we'll gather those.
[14:31] Marco Ruiz: thanks, this was helpful. We'll aim to share logs by end of day tomorrow.
[14:36] Sara Kim: great, Liam will send the config and flags, Priya will include notes on quantization kernels, and I'll coordinate the bench schedule.
[14:45] Priya Nair: one more note — consider enabling conservative KD-quant fallback: if kernel allocation fails, route to a smaller context model variant rather than retrying on same node. That avoids OOM storms.
[14:58] Vikram Patel: good idea.
[15:00] Sara Kim: ok we'll wrap here. Thanks everyone.

References mentioned: kernel selection flags, TORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF, nvml, cuBLAS, NCCL, cublas allocation failures, kv cache, idempotency tokens, admission control.

Links shared / artifacts: (to be sent) debug-config.yaml, kernel-policy.csv, sample CUDA OOM logs (redacted), bench-replay-instructions.md
